title: The history of motion capture
tagline: From a galloping horse and a man in a striped suit to creatures that act live on set: 150 years of turning movement into numbers.
intro: People first studied movement with photographs, then traced it by hand. Psychologists showed that a few moving dots are enough to see a person. Gait labs, games and then films built systems that turn those dots into 3D skeletons, and actors learned to perform creatures. Today capture works outdoors, underwater, and with no suit at all.

eras.name: Photographing and tracing motion
eras.summary: Muybridge and Marey take movement apart with cameras. Marey's black suit with white lines is the first marker suit. Fleischer and Disney trace real performers onto drawn characters.

eras.name: Dots, lights and computers
eras.summary: Johansson shows a few moving lights read as a person. Labs and gait clinics build camera systems that triangulate markers, and games and adverts start using them.

eras.name: Performance capture
eras.summary: Mocap drives main characters. Gollum makes it acting, The Polar Express shoots a whole film on a stage, and Avatar adds head-mounted cameras and a virtual camera.

eras.name: Capture anywhere
eras.summary: Capture moves outdoors and underwater, game engines make it real time, and machine learning finds poses in ordinary video and phones.

events.title: A galloping horse, frozen in 12 photos
events.text: Muybridge lined up a row of cameras beside a racetrack. Threads across the track fired the shutters one after another as the horse ran past, catching each phase of its stride.
events.why: It proved that a camera could take movement apart, and showed that all four hooves leave the ground at once.

events.title: A camera shaped like a rifle
events.text: Marey, a doctor who studied how animals move, built a chronophotographic gun that took 12 pictures a second, all from one viewpoint, to study birds in flight.
events.why: Measuring motion from many timed pictures is exactly what a mocap camera still does, only faster.

events.title: The first marker suit
events.text: Marey dressed a man in black with thin white stripes and dots along his arms and legs, then photographed him walking and running in front of a black wall. Only the white lines showed, so each photo became a moving stick figure.
events.why: Black suit, bright marks, dark background: it is the idea behind every optical marker suit today.

events.title: The rotoscope
events.who: Max Fleischer, with his brother Dave
events.text: Fleischer projected film of a real person, one frame at a time, onto glass and traced it onto paper. Dave Fleischer, dressed as a clown, was the reference for Koko the Clown in Out of the Inkwell.
events.why: Copying a real performer's movement into a drawn character is the goal of motion capture, done by hand.

events.title: Real dancers behind Snow White
events.text: After Fleischer's patent ran out, Disney animators filmed live actors and used rotoscoping as reference for Snow White and the Prince, to make their movement look human.
events.why: It showed that audiences read real human motion as more believable, a big reason mocap exists.

events.title: A person made of 10 to 12 lights
events.text: Johansson fixed small lights to an actor's main joints and filmed them moving in the dark. When the dots were still, viewers saw a random pattern. The moment they moved, people instantly saw someone walking, running or dancing.
events.why: It proved that a few moving points hold most of what we read in body movement, which is why a few dozen markers can capture a performance.

events.title: The Graphical Marionette
events.who: Carol Ginsberg and Delle Maxwell, MIT
events.text: A performer wore a suit with LEDs on the joints. Two cameras with special light sensors each reported the 2D position of every LED, and a computer combined them into 3D points that drove a stick figure live.
events.why: It was triangulation from two cameras driving a digital character, the core of optical mocap.

events.title: Measuring how children walk
events.who: Vicon, Oxford Metrics (Julian Morris and team)
events.text: Vicon's early camera systems were built for clinical gait analysis: measuring how children with cerebral palsy walk before and after surgery. Hospitals and universities helped set standard ways of placing markers.
events.why: Medicine came first. The marker sets and methods that films use grew out of gait labs.

events.title: A shiny robot in a Super Bowl ad
events.text: For the advert Brilliance, the team filmed a real actress with reference points marked on her body, and a computer tracked those points to move a chrome computer-graphics robot.
events.why: It was one of the first times captured human motion drove a CG character on television.

events.title: Skeletons through an X-ray screen
events.text: For the scene where people walk behind an airport X-ray scanner, the team recorded the actors with motion capture to animate glowing CG skeletons. Accounts differ on how much of the capture data ended up in the final shots.
events.why: It is often named as an early feature-film use of motion capture.

events.title: Fighters that move like people
events.text: Sega's arcade games Virtua Fighter and Virtua Fighter 2 used motion capture to animate their 3D fighters. Soon many studios built their own capture stages for games.
events.why: Games became one of the biggest users of mocap, and still are.

events.title: A main character from mocap
events.who: Ahmed Best and Industrial Light & Magic
events.where: London, UK and San Rafael, USA
events.text: Star Wars: Episode I featured Jar Jar Binks, the first main character in a feature film created with motion capture from an actor's performance.
events.why: Mocap moved from background extras to a leading role.

events.title: A whole film made with mocap, animated in Chennai
events.where: Chennai (then Madras), India, and Los Angeles, USA
events.text: Sinbad: Beyond the Veil of Mists was the first feature-length computer-animated film made with motion capture. Actors were captured in Los Angeles in 1997, and a couple of hundred animators in Madras built the film.
events.why: An Indian studio led the first full-length mocap film, years before Hollywood's big ones.

events.title: Realistic digital humans
events.text: Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within aimed for photorealistic human characters, animated with motion capture. It was the first widely released film made this way.
events.why: It showed how hard it is to make digital humans feel alive, even with real motion.

events.title: Gollum and Andy Serkis
events.text: Serkis acted Gollum on set with the other actors, then again in a marker suit on a capture stage. In The Two Towers his body motion streamed live onto the CG Gollum; animators used his face and voice as the guide for Gollum's face.
events.why: It turned mocap into acting. People began to talk about performance capture and the actor behind the creature.

events.title: A whole film shot on a capture stage
events.who: Robert Zemeckis, Sony Pictures Imageworks and Vicon
events.text: The Polar Express used 72 cameras around a capture area about 10 feet (3 m) square. Up to four actors were captured together, bodies and faces: each wore about 48 body markers and 152 small face markers.
events.why: It was the first film shot entirely on a motion-capture stage, and showed face capture's promise and problems.

events.title: Kong's face from 135 markers
events.text: For King Kong, Serkis studied gorillas at London Zoo and in Rwanda. He had 135 small markers glued to his face, about two hours of make-up a day, to drive the ape's expressions.
events.why: Face markers mapped a human face onto a very different creature face, a big step in retargeting.

events.title: Head rigs and a virtual camera
events.who: James Cameron, Lightstorm and Weta Digital
events.where: Los Angeles, USA and Wellington, New Zealand
events.text: For Avatar, actors wore skull caps with a tiny camera on a boom in front of the face, instead of hundreds of glued markers. Cameron used a virtual camera to see the Na'vi in Pandora live, on a capture stage described as six times larger than any before.
events.why: The head-mounted camera and virtual camera became standard tools of performance capture.

events.title: Apes captured outdoors
events.who: Weta Digital, with Andy Serkis as Caesar
events.where: Vancouver, Canada and San Francisco, USA
events.text: Rise of the Planet of the Apes took performance capture out of the studio onto real locations, including a battle on a Golden Gate Bridge set. A camera that could see the capture markers in daylight made it possible.
events.why: Mocap no longer needed a dark stage; creatures could act beside live actors on real sets.

events.title: India's first photorealistic mocap film
events.where: Chennai, India, and Pinewood Studios, London, UK
events.text: Kochadaiiyaan was captured at the Centroid lab at Pinewood Studios with 48 cameras, and Rajinikanth performed his triple role in a marker suit. Big Indian effects films such as Ra.One (2011) and Baahubali (2015) also leaned on VFX, though published accounts say little about how much mocap each used.
events.why: It was billed as India's first photorealistic motion-capture feature.

events.title: From capture to final shot in minutes
events.who: Ninja Theory, Epic Games, Cubic Motion and 3Lateral
events.text: On stage at SIGGRAPH, actress Melina Juergens performed as Senua from the game Hellblade. Her body and face were captured and rendered live in a game engine, then cut into a finished scene in minutes. It won Best Real-Time Graphics and Interactivity.
events.why: Game engines made real-time performance capture good enough to be close to final.

events.title: OpenPose: skeletons from any video
events.who: Zhe Cao, Yaser Sheikh and team, Carnegie Mellon University
events.text: OpenPose was the first open-source system to find the body keypoints of many people in ordinary video in real time, using deep learning and part affinity fields.
events.why: It started the markerless wave: pose from video, no suit.

events.title: Face capture in a phone
events.text: The iPhone X's TrueDepth camera projects over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the face. Apple's ARKit turns them into 52 blend-shape weights, such as jaw open and brow up, many times a second.
events.why: Facial capture that once needed a studio became something anyone could try at home.

events.title: 33 body points on a phone
events.who: Valentin Bazarevsky and team, Google Research
events.text: BlazePose found 33 body landmarks in real time on a mobile phone, using only its ordinary camera.
events.why: Markerless capture shrank from a computer lab to a pocket.

events.title: How accurate is markerless?
events.text: A study compared OpenPose with several video cameras against a marker system. About 80% of joint errors were under 30 mm, but some were over 40 mm. Markers still win when millimetres matter.
events.why: It measured the trade-off: markerless is easy and cheap, optical is precise.

events.title: Inertial suits on an Indian epic
events.text: The motion-capture shoot for Adipurush began in January 2021 with Xsens inertial suits for the body, and a separate head-mounted system for faces.
events.why: Inertial suits let big Indian productions capture without a huge optical stage.

events.title: Performance capture underwater
events.who: James Cameron, Lightstorm and Wētā FX
events.text: For Avatar: The Way of Water, the team captured actors underwater in a huge tank built at Manhattan Beach Studios (reports of its size vary). Air bubbles act as tiny wiggling mirrors that fool the cameras, so actors and crew held their breath while performing.
events.why: Capture moved into places once thought impossible for optical systems.

people.name: Étienne-Jules Marey
people.note: Dressed a man in black with white stripes to photograph movement as a stick figure.

people.name: Max Fleischer
people.note: Invented the rotoscope to trace real motion into cartoons.

people.name: Gunnar Johansson
people.note: Showed that a dozen moving lights are enough to see a person walking.

people.name: Andy Serkis
people.note: Played Gollum, Kong and Caesar, and made performance capture a craft of acting.

people.name: Rajinikanth
people.note: Performed a triple role in a marker suit for Kochadaiiyaan, India's first photorealistic mocap film.

series.title: Cameras watching the performers
series.caption: Two light sensors in 1983 grew to dozens of cameras on big film stages (SIGGRAPH, AWN, Wikipedia).

facts: A mocap camera does not record a picture of the actor. It sends only the centres of bright dots, often 120 times a second or more.
A lab test of one optical system measured an average error of just 0.15 mm for a still marker.
Johansson's viewers recognised a walking person from about a dozen moving lights, but saw only random dots when the lights stood still.
On The Polar Express, each actor wore about 200 markers, 152 of them on the face, and 72 cameras watched up to four actors at once.
An iPhone's face camera projects more than 30,000 invisible dots to measure the shape of your face.
